newsitem.title: USA: Challenge to San Diego stadium plan dismissed.
newsitem.headline: Challenge to San Diego stadium plan dismissed.

text.p: A Superior Court judge Thursday dismissed a lawsuit challenging San Diego's $78 million stadium expansion project, clearing the way for the Super Bowl to be played here in 1998.
The National Football League (NFL) had announced a contingency plan to hold the sports event at the Rose Bowl in Pasadena, Calif., if stadium construction was halted because of the suit.
In addition, the San Diego Chargers football team said it would have to play elsewhere, probably in Los Angeles, if improvements to San Diego Jack Murphy Stadium were halted.
Stadium opponents argued it was illegal for the city to start construction in December, before completion of a petition drive which would put the project to a public vote.
But Judge Anthony Joseph ruled it did not matter because a 1995 agreement between the city and the Chargers to expand the stadium was already in force.

That original deal for $60 million grew to $78 million because of delays, so in December the city council passed an amendment to finance the additional cost. The council, however, later rescinded that amendment.

Attorneys for a group of private citizens who brought the lawsuit argued the city's action nullified the whole deal, while attorneys for the city contended the plaintiffs' action was groundless because the amendment was no longer in force.
Joseph concluded that the council's repeal of the ordinance "did not affect the validity of the 1995 agreement or any other legislative act concerning the stadium or the Chargers."

NFL Commissioner Paul Tagliabue said the NFL was pleased by the ruling. "With construction going forward on schedule, the uncertainty regarding the condition of the stadium has been removed and we can proceed with plans to play Super Bowl XXXII in Jack Murphy Stadium."
"We look forward to a great Super Bowl week next January in the San Diego area," he said in a statement.

Bruce Henderson, the main plaintiff in the case, said afterwards that "the stadium battle is not over." While attorneys said they will not appeal, Henderson said he will monitor aspects of the contract such as the city's agreement to guarantee a certain amount of ticket sales. "I don't know where the city is going to come up with the money to complete the $78 million," he added.

The initial $60 million is being financed through the sale of lease revenue bonds. Last week, Qualcomm Inc., a local firm, offered to put up the additional $18 million in exchange for its name on the stadium. The matter is still being considered by council.

"It's time to move forward," Councilman George Stevens said after the hearing. "Tourism is a big part of this city and sports is a big part of that. And, of course, the stadium is a big part of sports in San Diego."
